page_title: Version numbers: how to use them?

sources.entry: Version numbers: how to use them?

summary.title: Version numbers: how to use them?
summary.one_liner: Semantic versioning often fails small-maintainer libraries by pinning users out of fixes and causing version conflicts, so the author argues for CalVer plus time-window deprecation warnings.
keywords: what version number should i use for my library
takeaways: Semantic versioning (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH) signals compatibility, but with few maintainers, only the latest release is effectively supported, so pinning to a major version blocks fixes.
Major version pins cause transitive dependency conflicts in Python, where only one version of a library can be installed at a time.
CalVer (YEAR.MONTH.sequence) makes release age explicit and fits the single-supported-version reality better.
Pair API changes with a time-window deprecation policy (e.g. one year of warnings) instead of major bumps.
Libraries should declare minimum versions only; applications should add a lock file with exact pins.
summary.summary: The article explains why version numbers matter for both library producers and consumers, then reviews semantic versioning and ZeroVer. It argues that semver breaks down for under-resourced maintainers: only the latest release gets fixes, major-version pins hold back security and bug fixes, and transitive dependencies create conflicts, illustrated with a tenacity example. It presents CalVer as an alternative and proposes Hynek Schlawack's approach of deprecation windows with warnings, ending with a summary of trade-offs and recommendations like minimum-only constraints and lock files for applications.
